wa_the_tooth_fairy.rappels: 6 single-rope rappels down the bolted line from the top of pitch 6, or 3 double-rope rappels; alternatively rappel the South Face to Pineapple Pass
wa_the_tooth_fairy.descent_text: From the top of P6 (the anchor is unequipped at the true summit — P7 is a short scramble with no rappel anchor), rappel the bolted line: 6 single-rope rappels, or 3 double-rope rappels with a 60m rope for the longest one. Some parties instead go down the South Face, rappelling its line to Pineapple Pass.

wa_the_tooth_indentured_servant.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on a single 60 m rope used doubled, each under 30 m, reversing the four pitches back to Pineapple Pass - this is what almost every party does and how the stations are spaced. Two 60 m ropes let you link them into fewer, longer rappels. One 60 m rappel in the sequence comes up just short of the next tree, leaving a short unroped downscramble, which an added pitch-3 anchor now avoids. A separate, partly hidden bolted line beside pitches 1 and 2 exists so that ascending and descending parties are not in the same place; it is a different set of anchors, not a variation. Below Pineapple Pass the east gully holds two more bolted chain stations for two further rappels on a 60 m - optional, and many parties scramble out instead; there is meaningful rockfall hazard in that gully. Do not scramble directly up to Pineapple Pass on the way in: that ground is the rappel route.

wa_the_tooth_south_face.rappels: 4 rappels (roughly 25-30m / under 100ft each) from slung tree, horn and block anchors back down to Pineapple Pass; many parties link them into fewer rappels with a single 60m rope.

wa_summit_chief_mountain_north_face.rappels: 2 x 30m rappels down the descent snow gully on the southwest side
wa_summit_chief_mountain_north_face.rappel_count_note: Two rappels of about 30 m down the snow gully on the southwest side are the reported descent. No fixed anchors are reported, so plan to build them.

wa_the_chopping_block_northeast_ridge.rappel_count_note: One party made four single-rope rappels and one double-rope rappel down the ridge, and judged three singles and a double would do. Which rappel needs the second rope is not recorded. A 70 m rope is recommended.
wa_the_chopping_block_northeast_ridge.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the ridge itself — most parties use a 70m rope to reach most stations comfortably; one reporting party got down on a 50m rope with a tagline. Existing fixed rap slings have been reported along the route.

Third double-rope rappel to the base. To skip the walk around the tower, a shorter way down takes two double-rope rappels westward down the cliff close to the base.

ut_finger_of_fate.rappels: Descend the line to the Duck, then make three raps in the gully to reach the base; a pair of double-rope raps on the western cliff close to the foot is a shortcut.

rappel_detail.notes: Third rappel, which some parties skip by downclimbing; it reaches easier 3rd-class ground above the glacier. Two ropes let parties link stations in fewer pulls.

wa_three_fingers_r1.rappel_count_note: Parties describe two to three rappels through the chimney-and-ramp section, on a single 60 m rope. The first anchor is usually old fixed tat; expect to build natural anchors for the rest. Lengths are not published.
wa_three_fingers_r1.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line off the North Peak summit. Parties describe two to three rappels getting back down through the 4th/low-5th-class chimney-and-ramp section to easier 3rd-class ground above the glacier — plan on a single 60m rope (or two ropes if parties want to link stations in fewer pulls). The first rappel station is commonly an old fixed sling/tat anchor left by previous parties, but it should not be trusted blindly — inspect it or back it up, and be prepared to build natural gear anchors (cams/nuts on horns or cracks) for the remaining stations since fixed gear is inconsistent year to year. After the rappels, downclimb/scramble the remaining 3rd-class terrain back to the col, reverse the ~1,000 ft descent to the glacier, re-cross the Queest-Alb Glacier (watch the moat and any crevasses), climb back up to Tin Can Gap, and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. Rockfall in the chimney/gully and a icy glacier moat are the main descent-specific hazards; a mid-to-late-season descent in soft/rotten snow on the glacier headwall can also be tricky.
